question: In 2019, the YouTube science series “Because Science” had Olympic sprinter Jeneba Tarmoh try this running style over a 50-meter dash. The experiment clocked it about three percent slower than her ordinary sprint, largely because it removes a runner’s arm counterbalance. The pose actually predates the anime that popularized it, having already been used to depict sprinting ninja in Japanese films and television of the 1960s and 70s. It became a nationwide talking point in the United States in September 2019, after thousands of people “signed up” online to raid a secretive Nevada Air Force base. Many of them joked that they would cross its perimeter using exactly this running style. Practitioners lean their torso forward and swing both arms straight out behind them at hip height instead of pumping them normally. For 10 points, name this sprinting style named for a spiky-haired, orange-jumpsuited ninja protagonist.

Attached to “nin,” this word names the historical ninja arts of stealth, infiltration and combat. Attached to “tai” instead, it names an unarmed martial art built on body movement rather than throws or strikes. In the ninja anime “Naruto,” sword-fighting’s “kenjutsu” and the illusion-casting “genjutsu” — a signature ability of one clan of antagonists — both end in this word too. That same anime conventionally names its techniques with this word attached. Its blond ninja hero shouts the name of his signature shadow-clone technique before a puff of smoke reveals dozens of copies of himself. Fans have jokingly appended “Talk no” to this word to describe that hero’s habit of ending fights with a heartfelt speech instead of violence. For 10 points, give this Japanese word for “technique” or “art,” also combined with “ju” to name a grappling martial art and its anime-fueled modern cousin.

This character’s iconic hat was given to him at age seven by Red-Haired Shanks, a former crewmate of the pirate king Gol D. Roger. Shanks told him to return the hat once he became a great pirate. Guinness World Records recognized “One Piece,” the manga starring this character, for surpassing 500 million copies printed by a single author as of 2022. In a 2023 anime episode whose wild, cartoonish art style fans both praised and mocked, this character unlocks “Gear Fifth” by awakening his Devil Fruit’s true form. That form is the mythical “Sun God Nika”. As a child, he unknowingly ate the Gum-Gum Fruit, which turned his body to rubber. For 10 points, name this rubber-limbed pirate captain, who leads the Straw Hat Pirates in a quest to become the Pirate King, and who is nicknamed for his straw hat.

A 2011 physics paper modeling cultural spread used this word and its Kansai-region rival “aho” as a case study, since the two insults radiate outward from Kyoto in concentric rings. That pattern echoes folklorist Kunio Yanagita’s 1930 “concentric circle theory” of Japanese dialect distribution, which places older word forms farthest from Kyoto. In the 1980s, English-speaking fans of the anime “Urusei Yatsura” began pairing a character’s name with this word as an injoke. They had borrowed the phrase from alien schoolgirl Lum, who would shout it at her boyfriend before shocking him with lightning. A 2010 school comedy anime takes its English title from this word paired with “and Test,” set among students whose exam scores summon battle avatars. Typically translated as “idiot” or “fool,” this word is a mainstay insult shouted by tsundere anime characters at their crush. For 10 points, give this common Japanese put-down.

Voice actress Saki Fujita recorded the vocal samples used to build this character’s software voicebank for Yamaha’s Vocaloid2 engine, released by Crypton Future Media on August 31, 2007. Illustrator KEI, who has said he did not know what a synthesizer was beforehand, designed this character’s turquoise twin-tails and schoolgirl outfit around Yamaha’s signature blue-green color scheme. Fans created a chibi, doll-eyed spinoff of this character after she appeared shaking a leek in a 2007 music video for a cover of the Finnish folk song “Ievan Polkka”. That leek-spinning meme had actually begun the previous year with an unrelated anime clip. In 2014, she appeared as a 3D hologram opening act on more than a dozen North American stops of Lady Gaga’s “ArtRave: The Artpop Ball” tour. Her name combines Japanese words for “first,” “sound” and “future”. For 10 points, name this turquoise-haired virtual idol, the flagship character of the Vocaloid singing-synthesizer software.

This franchise’s first giant robot was originally going to be called “Freedom Fighter Gunboy” during its 1979 development at the animation studio Sunrise. Directed by Yoshiyuki Tomino, its debut TV series established the “real robot” subgenre of mecha anime, favoring mass-produced military hardware over a single invincible hero machine. A moving, 18-meter, 25-ton statue of this franchise’s original robot stood in Yokohama from 2020 until 2024. It was then dismantled for display, arm raised to the sky, at the 2025 World Expo in Osaka. A similar giant statue has also stood on the artificial island of Odaiba, including a temporary model built for the franchise’s 30th anniversary in 2009. Its giant humanoid “mobile suits” are piloted in interstellar wars, and its toy model kits are nicknamed “Gunpla”. For 10 points, name this influential mecha anime and toy franchise that debuted in Japan in 1979.

Since 1973, this intersection has let pedestrians cross diagonally from every corner at once when its lights change, instead of only in an L-shaped pattern. It has been described as the world’s busiest pedestrian crossing, with estimates of up to three thousand people crossing during a single green-light cycle. Sofia Coppola filmed here repeatedly for her 2003 film “Lost in Translation,” including a rain-soaked scene where Scarlett Johansson’s character walks through a sea of translucent umbrellas. It sits outside a train station plaza that also holds a bronze statue of a famously loyal dog, a popular meeting spot for visitors. Overlooked by giant video screens and a busy Starbucks with a bird’s-eye view, it is often compared to New York’s Times Square. For 10 points, name this famously chaotic Tokyo pedestrian crossing.

During this event, Kenjaku — secretly inhabiting the body of sorcerer Suguru Geto — traps Satoru Gojo inside the “Prison Realm” cursed object. That seals away the world’s strongest sorcerer for the next nineteen days. It unfolds on Halloween night of 2018, when a curtain-like barrier drops over a Tokyo entertainment district. That barrier forces student and professional sorcerers into a series of increasingly desperate battles against special-grade curses. Adapting this arc, the second season of “Jujutsu Kaisen” aired in 2023 to a wave of viral reaction videos, as fans watched beloved characters suffer devastating losses in real time. It takes its name from the same crowded shopping and nightlife district as a famous scramble crossing located just blocks from where its worst battles take place. For 10 points, name this Halloween 2018 attack in “Jujutsu Kaisen,” in which Gojo Satoru gets trapped inside a small box.

According to the University of Tokyo, this dog likely waited for his owner at their campus gate during his owner’s lifetime, not at the station most depictions show. His owner, agriculture professor Hidesaburō Ueno, died of a cerebral hemorrhage in May 1925. The dog then began returning each evening to that station to wait, for nearly ten more years until his own death. He was named for the character meaning “eight,” reportedly because his forelegs formed that shape when he stood as a puppy. He personally attended the unveiling of his own bronze statue outside that station in April 1934, about a year before he died. His preserved body has been on permanent display at Tokyo’s National Museum of Nature and Science since shortly after his 1935 death. For 10 points, name this Akita dog famed for his loyalty to a Tokyo professor.
